Well, yes, I suppose that’s a big part of it. It’s funny you use the word afraid, because I don't think of myself as a fearful person, generally speaking. And then I start thinking about how I need to make up for it. I'll tell myself I have to scrub the floors on the entire second level by hand instead of using the machine, or I'll walk the long way home, just to sort of... erase it, I guess? It’s exhausting, really, being so scared of just a little bit of food turning into weight, but I just can't seem to shake the feeling once it starts.

Well, "fat" is such a harsh word, isn't it? I don't know if I walk around thinking the exact word *fat*, but... well, people do say I'm too thin. Dr. Henderson, obviously, and my sister-in-law Martha—she calls every Sunday evening just to ask what I've eaten, which drives me absolutely up the wall, and she's always saying I'm fading away. But the thing is, when I look at myself, I just don't see what they see. I really don't. 

For me, it's more about being... tidy. I’ve always prided myself on being a tidy person, you know? Keeping a neat house, doing a thorough job at the college, making sure the baseboards are dusted, everything in its proper place. And that extends to my own body. When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s like, as long as I take up less space and my clothes are loose, my life is in order and I'm coping with everything since my husband passed. 

But if I happen to catch my reflection—like in that big full-length mirror in the faculty restroom on the third floor, the one with that awful, harsh fluorescent lighting that just highlights absolutely every single flaw—if I look in there and my stomach looks the least bit full, even just from drinking a glass of water or having a few bites of something, I just panic. I look at it and I feel like I've completely let myself go. It doesn't matter what Martha or the doctor says about my weight or my BMI or whatever, in that moment, I just feel so sloppy and out of control. I see so many women my age just sort of give up, you know? They start wearing those elastic waistbands and big flowy tunics to hide their middles, and I just... I can't be like that. I refuse to be like that. I can't let myself go. So when they tell me I'm too thin, I always just think, well, you aren't looking at my stomach in the mirror after I've had something to eat, are you? Because if they did, they’d see exactly what I mean.

Well, it's not really a specific number I have written down somewhere, like a goal weight or anything like that. I don't keep a little chart or a diary. It's more of a... a feeling, I suppose? It's like, I know my pants don't fit and people are looking at me a little funny, but when the number is lower, I just feel this sense of... I don't know, accomplishment? Control? It's confusing, honestly, which I guess is why I'm sitting here talking to you.\n\nDoctor: When you feel relieved seeing the number on the scale go down, is it because you're afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose that’s a big part of it. But when it comes to this... yes, there's this underlying dread. It’s just, well, if I eat something heavier, you know? Like, the other day, one of the ladies from the administration office left a tin of biscuits in the breakroom—the really nice buttery ones from Marks & Spencer—and I had one with my tea. I look at it and I feel like I've completely let myself go. Well, Arthur’s passing... that was five years ago this coming November. It was very sudden, you know. We were just sitting in the living room, and... well, anyway. I suppose you could say that’s when things really took a turn. Before he died, I never really obsessed over every little thing I put in my mouth. And then my mind just races with all the ways I need to make up for it. I’ll tell myself I have to do the stairs in the science building twice, or scrub the grout in the restrooms until my knuckles ache. It’s just... when Arthur died, I couldn't control any of it. The whole world just fell out from under me and it was completely out of my hands. So now, if I eat something dense or heavy, I just get so incredibly scared that I'm losing my grip on this, too. I just have to do whatever it takes to make sure the food doesn't show on me. I just can't bear the thought of it.

Well, I suppose I must, mustn't I? Because, like I was trying to explain earlier about Martha and Dr. Henderson... they look at me and they see someone who is, I don't know, fading away, or someone who is unwell. But I just don't see that. When I look at myself, it's entirely different.

But then... oh, it's just so frustrating because people don't understand how quickly that image changes for me. If I have a glass of water, or if I eat something and then I happen to catch my reflection—like in that awful faculty restroom mirror, or even just the reflection in the glass of the display cases in the history department while I'm dusting them—if my stomach looks the least bit full, I don't see what Martha sees at all. I don't see someone who's "too thin." I just look at that little bit of roundness, that tiny bulge, and I feel like I've completely let myself go. I feel like a total failure in that moment, like I'm just sloppy and undisciplined and all my hard work of keeping things neat has just vanished. 

And I try to tell Martha this! I say, "Martha, you just aren't seeing me right after I've eaten, you aren't seeing how my stomach pushes out against my slacks," but she just sighs at me. She doesn't get it. She doesn't understand that the way I look to myself in those moments is just... it's unbearable. So yes, I do think we're seeing two completely different things. They see a number on a scale, I suppose, but I just see whether or not I'm keeping my life in order.

Well, it's funny you mention the scale, because... well, Dr. Henderson, my general practitioner, he's always telling me I've gotten too thin. He looks at my chart and shakes his head, and he's got this very serious tone he uses, like he's talking to a child who won't listen. And, you know, I do see what he means, in a practical sense. Like with my work uniform. The college issues us these heavy navy blue slacks—awful material, really stiff and unforgiving—and lately, they're just hanging off me. I have to pull my belt so tight that the fabric bunches up all around the waist, and it looks terrible, just so untidy. I spend half my shift hiking them up while I'm trying to mop the hallways. 

So I know, logically, that the number on the scale must be low. I know I've lost weight. But... and this is the part that's so hard to explain to Dr. Henderson or to Martha... when I actually step on the scale in my bathroom—it's this old digital one Arthur bought years ago, the battery cover is held on with a piece of scotch tape—when I look down and see that the number is lower, I don't feel worried. I don't think, "Oh dear, my pants won't fit." I just feel... relieved. It's this immense, washing wave of relief. It's like a little confirmation that I'm doing it right, that I'm keeping everything contained. 

Even if the doctor says it's too low, and even if my clothes are falling off, that lower number just feels like a victory. It feels safe. So I don't think the scale is lying, exactly, or that I weigh less than it says... it's just that what the scale says means something completely different to me than it does to anyone else. To them, it's a warning sign. To me, it's just... it's proof that I haven't let go of the reins.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, well... I suppose... I don't think taking away the mirrors would really change anything, to be completely honest with you. Because, you see, it’s not just about the physical act of looking, even though I know I just went on and on about checking my reflection in the glass doors and the bathroom mirrors. It’s the knowing. It’s that heavy feeling inside. 

Like I was trying to explain just a little bit ago, and I know I keep coming back to this, but if I eat something heavier, like one of those biscuits from the breakroom or a bowl of pasta... even if I were in a pitch-black room and couldn't see a thing, I would still spend the entire rest of the day just absolutely scared to death that it’s going to show on me. 

Because even if I couldn't see my body with my eyes, my mind would still be doing the exact same thing. I'd still be checking myself, just in different ways. I'd be feeling my stomach with my hands underneath my uniform, or pressing my arms tight against my sides while I'm emptying the trash bins, just desperately trying to gauge if I've gotten bigger or softer. The terror of it doesn't just vanish because I can't see it. I’d still be standing there thinking that I need to make up for it, feeling that awful, urgent pressure telling me I have to go scrub the baseboards in the library until my shoulders ache, or walk the perimeter of the campus just to be sure I'm fixing it. So, no, not seeing my body wouldn't stop the fear at all. The fear just takes over the second I swallow something dense, whether I can see myself or not.

Unattractive? Oh... no, I wouldn't use that word. It really isn't about being pretty or trying to look like some model in a magazine, if that's what you're getting at. It’s this overwhelming, crushing sense of failure, like I've become sloppy and careless, just like the students who leave their rubbish shoved into the cracks of the lecture hall seats. 

If I gain weight, it means I'm losing that discipline. It means I'm not doing my job of holding myself together. So the fear isn't about being unattractive to other people, it’s about that horrible, panicky feeling of unraveling, of not being neat and contained anymore. Yes, exactly. I know I just touched on that a moment ago, but that is really the absolute heart of it, isn't it? Control. That's a very good word for it. Well... larger than it actually is? I suppose... I mean, it’s a difficult thing to explain, and I know I keep circling back to this same point, but it really all comes down to what I see when I catch my reflection while I'm working. 

It’s like... well, when I stay small and neat, I look in the glass and I just feel this immense relief. I look at my reflection and I feel like I'm handling everything right, like I'm keeping all the pieces of my life tucked in exactly where they belong. It looks correct to me. It looks safe. 

But if I get scared that I've gained weight... say I've had a glass of water or a few bites of a sandwich in the breakroom... the way I see myself completely shifts. I know, logically, that a few bites of food don't add ten pounds in five minutes. I went to college for a couple of years, I'm not a foolish woman. I understand how biology works. But when that panic sets in, my eyes just lock onto my midsection, and if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror, it doesn't just look like a normal stomach anymore. It looks... it looks enormous to me. It feels like it’s just protruding and taking up all this space, completely out of proportion with the rest of me. 

And it’s in those moments, standing there under those harsh fluorescent lights in the staff restrooms, staring at that fullness... I just feel like I've completely let myself go. It feels like this massive, glaring evidence that I've lost my grip and become sloppy. Even if my uniform still buttons exactly the same way it did that morning, what I actually see in the mirror is this huge, heavy failure. It just expands in my mind until it's all I can focus on. So, yes, I do think I see it as much larger than it probably is, because the fear just distorts everything until all I can see is the mess I'm making of myself.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, I know I must be sounding like a broken record at this point, Doctor, because it feels like we're circling right back to the exact same thing again. But... yes. Shape, weight, size... it all just gets so terribly twisted up in my head when I stand in front of that glass.

The shape itself looks completely wrong to me. It looks heavy and cumbersome, and I immediately get that awful, sinking feeling that I've just completely let myself go. Even if the tag on my work slacks says they're the exact same size they were yesterday, the shape I see in the mirror is the shape of a woman who has given up, who is sloppy and careless. 

My mind just takes that tiny bit of fullness and magnifies it until it's the only thing I can see, and it completely overtakes the reality of what's actually there. I'll stand there rubbing a smudge off the mirror with my rag, just staring at myself, and the shape I see is absolutely dictated by that fear. So, yes, I suppose the shape I see is completely different from reality, because it's so tied up in whether I feel neat and capable, or whether I feel like I've let the mess win.

The terror of it doesn't just vanish because I can't see it. I’d still be standing there thinking that I need to make up for it, feeling that awful, urgent pressure telling me I have to go scrub the baseboards in the library until my shoulders ache, or walk the perimeter of the campus just to be sure I'm fixing it. So, no, not seeing my body wouldn't stop the fear at all. The fear just takes over the second I swallow something dense, whether I can see myself or not.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you believe you would look unattractive if you gained weight?\n\nPatient: Unattractive? Oh... no, I wouldn't use that word. It really isn't about being pretty or trying to look like some model in a magazine, if that's what you're getting at. I mean, I'm sixty-four years old and I spend my evenings scrubbing floors and wiping down chalkboards—people don't really look twice at the cleaning lady anyway, do they? We're practically invisible in those big university buildings. And I certainly aren't trying to catch anyone's eye. Arthur was my only love, and since he passed, well, vanity just hasn't been any sort of priority for me. \n\nSo, no, it's not about attractiveness at all. It’s really exactly what I was trying to explain to you earlier, when we were talking about catching my reflection in the glass. I know I'm repeating myself a bit here, but it really just boils down to keeping things in order. When I make sure that I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s like I have this tight grip on my life, keeping everything perfectly structured and tidy, just like how I have to organize my supply cart before a shift so the cleaning solutions don't spill. \n\nBut the second I see any change... if I look in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full, even if it's just from drinking a cup of tea or having a piece of toast in the breakroom, I don't think, \"Oh dear, I look ugly.\" I just feel like I've completely let myself go. It’s this overwhelming, crushing sense of failure, like I've become sloppy and careless, just like the students who leave their rubbish shoved into the cracks of the lecture hall seats. \n\nIf I gain weight, it means I'm losing that discipline. It means I'm not doing my job of holding myself together. So the fear isn't about being unattractive to other people, it’s about that horrible, panicky feeling of unraveling, of not being neat and contained anymore. To me, being small is just... it's being capable. It's proof that I haven't let the mess win.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like gaining weight would mean you're losing control of your life?\n\nPatient: Yes, exactly. I know I just touched on that a moment ago, but that is really the absolute heart of it, isn't it? Control. That's a very good word for it. Because, you see, after Arthur passed away, everything in my life just felt so... unmoored. Like it was all just floating away from me. The house suddenly felt entirely too big and too quiet, the bank statements were confusing, and I took this job at the university just to have somewhere to be, just to have something to do with my hands so I wouldn't sit in his armchair all day. \n\nAnd every evening I go in there, and I see these young students rushing around, spilling their coffees, leaving scuff marks all over the freshly waxed linoleum in the science building... it's just constant chaos. It's a constant, never-ending mess that other people make, and I'm the one who has to quietly follow behind and put it all back to rights. \n\nSo my own body... well, it’s the one thing, perhaps the very only thing left in my life, that I can keep perfectly in line. Like I was saying before, when I manage to stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. I feel like I'm steering the ship, so to speak. It tells me that I haven't succumbed to the chaos. \n\nBut the absolute second I step out of the shower and catch a glimpse of myself, if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror... oh, Doctor, it's just devastating. I don't just see a physical change. I feel like I've completely let myself go. I feel like I'm becoming just as careless and sloppy as the people who leave their trash on the library tables. If I were to actually gain weight, it would mean the mess had finally won. It would mean I wasn't capable of managing myself anymore. So, yes, keeping the weight off is... it's the only way I know I'm still holding on to the reins.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your body is larger than it actually is when you're afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well... larger than it actually is? I suppose... I mean, it’s a difficult thing to explain, and I know I keep circling back to this same point, but it really all comes down to what I see when I catch my reflection while I'm working. \n\nIt’s like... well, when I stay small and neat, I look in the glass and I just feel this immense relief. I look at my reflection and I feel like I'm handling everything right, like I'm keeping all the pieces of my life tucked in exactly where they belong. It looks correct to me. It looks safe. \n\nBut if I get scared that I've gained weight... say I've had a glass of water or a few bites of a sandwich in the breakroom... the way I see myself completely shifts. It looks... it looks enormous to me. So, yes, I do think I see it as much larger than it probably is, because the fear just distorts everything until all I can see is the mess I'm making of myself.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your body shape or weight is different from how it actually is when you look in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Well, I know I must be sounding like a broken record at this point, Doctor, because it feels like we're circling right back to the exact same thing again. But... yes. Shape, weight, size... it all just gets so terribly twisted up in my head when I stand in front of that glass. \n\nLike I was trying to explain just a moment ago, it all hinges on that reflection. As long as I can look in the mirror in the staff washroom and see that my shape is small and... well, tidy, I suppose... it just gives me this profound sense of relief. It reassures me that I'm doing things correctly. When I'm small and neat, it tells me I'm handling everything right in my life, that I'm keeping the chaos at bay. The shape I see when I'm empty is the shape of a woman who has her life properly organized. \n\nBut if I catch my reflection and there's even the slightest shift—if my stomach seems even a tiny bit rounder, or if I imagine my waist isn't perfectly straight—it’s not just a minor physical change I'm seeing. The shape itself looks completely wrong to me. It looks heavy and cumbersome, and I immediately get that awful, sinking feeling that I've just completely let myself go. Even if the tag on my work slacks says they're the exact same size they were yesterday, the shape I see in the mirror is the shape of a woman who has given up, who is sloppy and careless. \n\nMy mind just takes that tiny bit of fullness and magnifies it until it's the only thing I can see, and it completely overtakes the reality of what's actually there. I'll stand there rubbing a smudge off the mirror with my rag, just staring at myself, and the shape I see is absolutely dictated by that fear. So, yes, I suppose the shape I see is completely different from reality, because it's so tied up in whether I feel neat and capable, or whether I feel like I've let the mess win.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you have a distorted view of what you look like?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose that’s... I'd be a weeping, hysterical mess because the one thing keeping me anchored, the one thing keeping the sadness in check, would be gone. 

If my stomach gets round, the sadness gets big. The fear gets big. It's all connected. So, yes, if I were to gain weight, I firmly believe my emotions would just run entirely amok. I wouldn't be able to hold back the tears or the panic anymore, because I wouldn't have that physical proof that I'm still capable of holding it all together.

To me, being small is just... it's being capable. It's proof that I haven't let the mess win.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like gaining weight would mean you're losing control of your life?\n\nPatient: Yes, exactly. I know I just touched on that a moment ago, but that is really the absolute heart of it, isn't it? Control. That's a very good word for it. Because, you see, after Arthur passed away, everything in my life just felt so... unmoored. Like it was all just floating away from me. The house suddenly felt entirely too big and too quiet, the bank statements were confusing, and I took this job at the university just to have somewhere to be, just to have something to do with my hands so I wouldn't sit in his armchair all day. \n\nAnd every evening I go in there, and I see these young students rushing around, spilling their coffees, leaving scuff marks all over the freshly waxed linoleum in the science building... it's just constant chaos. It's a constant, never-ending mess that other people make, and I'm the one who has to quietly follow behind and put it all back to rights. \n\nSo my own body... well, it’s the one thing, perhaps the very only thing left in my life, that I can keep perfectly in line. Like I was saying before, when I manage to stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. I feel like I'm steering the ship, so to speak. It tells me that I haven't succumbed to the chaos. \n\nBut the absolute second I step out of the shower and catch a glimpse of myself, if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror... oh, Doctor, it's just devastating. I don't just see a physical change. I feel like I've completely let myself go. I feel like I'm becoming just as careless and sloppy as the people who leave their trash on the library tables. Oh, Doctor, I feel dreadful because I'm just circling right back to the exact same thing again. You must think I only have one thought in my lonely old head, and I know I'm taking up so much of your time with my rambling today, but... yes. Yes, that's exactly it. Coping with my daily life is the whole battle, isn't it? 

People think my life is simple now, but it's really not. Waking up in that desperately quiet house without Arthur, making my tea for one, putting on my heavy work uniform, driving to the campus in the pitch dark, dealing with the bills, the endless silence... all of those things are my daily challenges. And just like I've been saying to you all afternoon, my ability to handle every single one of those things is completely, entirely tied to my size. 

It's just as I was explaining before—when I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. I feel equipped to push my heavy cart down those long corridors, to empty the bins, to just get through another night on my own. I feel capable. But if I happen to catch my reflection in the glass of the double doors by the science lab, and if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror... well, I feel like I've let myself go. 

And if I've let myself go physically, how on earth am I supposed to cope with everything else? It feels like the wheels would just fall right off the wagon. If I can't even keep my own body disciplined and tidy, I certainly wouldn't be able to handle the grief or the loneliness or even just the basic tasks of my job. The weight is the only thing I have a strict handle on. So if I were to gain weight, yes, I firmly believe I wouldn't be able to cope with a single thing in my life anymore. It would all just fall apart.
